objectives.label: Measure arcs from central angles
objectives.description: Determine the measure of an arc as the measure of its central angle, and find the measures of adjacent arcs, semicircles and the circle by adding or subtracting.

objectives.label: Calculate arc length
objectives.description: Calculate the length of an arc as the fraction (measure of the arc / measure of the circle) of the circumference, and compare arcs of equal measure in different circles.

objectives.label: Relate arcs, chords and parallels
objectives.description: Use the corollaries on equal arcs, equal chords and parallel chords or tangents to prove arcs or chords are equal and to find unknown lengths.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: The two sides of angle AMB divide the circle M into two arcs:

A.why: Introduces what an arc is: the two sides of the central angle divide the circle into two arcs.

B.why: Introduces the idea that the sides of a central angle divide the circle into two arcs.

passages.text: What is the position of the points of arc AB with respect to angle AMB?

A.why: A figure-based question asking the student to observe, not a reflection.

B.why: Asks the student to observe a figure position.

passages.text: What is the position of points of arc ACB with respect to reflected angle of angle AMB?

A.why: A figure-based observation question.

B.why: Asks the student to observe a figure position.

passages.text: If angle AMB is a straight angle, what do you notice?

A.why: A figure-based observation question about the straight angle.

B.why: Asks the student to observe a figure; it is an exploration prompt.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: AB is a diameter in the circle M, MC ⊥ AB, m(∠AMD) = 60°.

A.why: Sets up a worked example's figure data.

B.why: Figure data for an example.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: AB is a diameter in the circle M, m(∠AMC) = 60°, m(∠AMD) = 40°.

A.why: Sets up a worked example's figure data.

B.why: Figure data for an example.

passages.text: Is $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ congruent to $\overset{\frown}{EF}$? What do you deduce?

A.why: Asks the student to compare arcs and deduce, which is work to do, not a look back.

B.why: Asks the student to work out a comparison from a figure, not a reflection.

passages.text: If: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$ then: the length of $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ = the length of $\overset{\frown}{CD}$

A.why: A rule restated.

B.why: A restated rule connecting arc measure and length.

passages.text: If: the length of $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ = the length of $\overset{\frown}{CD}$ then: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$

A.why: A rule restated.

B.why: A restated rule connecting arc length and measure.

passages.text: If: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$ then: length of $\overline{AB}$ = length of $\overline{CD}$

A.why: A corollary restated.

B.why: A restated corollary on equal arcs and chords.

passages.text: If: $AB = CD$ then: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$

A.why: A corollary restated.

B.why: A restated corollary on equal chords.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 60^\circ$ et $m(\overset{\frown}{BC}) = 80^\circ$, $m(\overset{\frown}{AD}) : m(\overset{\frown}{DC}) = 4 : 7$

A.why: Figure data for an example.

B.why: Figure data for an example with numbers.

passages.text: If $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are two chords in circle M, $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}$ then: $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = m(\overset{\frown}{BD})$.

A.why: A corollary statement.

B.why: A restated corollary on parallel chords.

passages.text: If $\overline{AB}$ is a chord of circle M, $\overleftrightarrow{CD}$ is a tangent at c, $\overline{AB} \parallel \overleftrightarrow{CD}$ then $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = m(\overset{\frown}{BC})$.

A.why: A corollary statement.

B.why: A restated corollary about a chord parallel to a tangent, not an introduction.

lessons.title: The relation between the inscribed and central angles subtended by the same arc

objectives.label: Inscribed and central angle relation
objectives.description: Calculate the measure of an inscribed angle or of the central angle subtended by the same arc, using the theorem that the inscribed angle is half the central angle.

objectives.label: Inscribed angle and arc measure
objectives.description: Calculate an inscribed angle from its subtended arc, find arc measures from angles, and show that an angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

objectives.label: Angles from intersecting chords and rays
objectives.description: Calculate the angle formed by two chords intersecting inside a circle, or by two rays intersecting outside it, using half the sum or half the difference of the intercepted arcs.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: What is the number of inscribed angles subtended with the central $\angle AMB$ at $\overset{\frown}{AB}$? (Clarify your answer with a drawing)

A.why: Opens the idea of inscribed angles sharing an arc with a central angle, with no numbers.

B.why: Asks the student to count and draw inscribed angles, which is a task, not a why-introduction.

passages.text: Given: $\angle ACB$ is an inscribed angle, $\angle AMB$ is a central angle.

A.why: Given statement of a proof.

B.why: The 'Given' part of the proof layout.

passages.text: R.T.P.: Prove that $m(\angle ACB) = \frac{1}{2} m(\angle AMB)$.

A.why: States what is to be proved, part of the proof.

B.why: The statement of what is to be proved, part of the proof layout.

passages.text: Proof: There are three cases to prove this theorem.

A.why: Proof setup line.

B.why: A proof heading line.

passages.text: Since $\angle AMB$ is outside $\Delta AMC$; therefore $m(\angle AMB) = m(\angle A) + m(\angle C)$ (1). Since $AM = CM$ (radii lengths), therefore $m(\angle A) = m(\angle C)$ (2). From (1) and (2) we get: $m(\angle AMB = 2\, m(\angle C)$; therefore $m(\angle ACB) = \frac{1}{2} m(\angle AMB)$ (Q.E.D)

A.why: Step of the worked proof.

B.why: A step of the theorem's proof.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: m(∠C) = 1/2 m(∠AMB), m(∠AMB) = m(arc AB), therefore m(∠C) = 1/2 m(arc AB).

A.why: Introduces that an inscribed angle is half its subtended arc.

B.why: A step in deriving the inscribed angle and arc relation.

passages.text: i.e.: If the arc opposite to the inscribed angle equals the semicircle then: m(∠C) = 1/2 m(arc AB). Since m(arc AB) = 180°, therefore m(∠C) = 90°.

A.why: Worked consequence for the semicircle, with numbers.

B.why: A worked step showing the semicircle case with numbers.

passages.text: What is the type of the inscribed angle opposite to an arc less than a semicircle? Why?

A.why: Asks the student to work out the angle type; not a reflection.

B.why: Asks the student to work out the angle type for a minor arc, so it is a task.

passages.text: What is the type of the inscribed angle opposite to an arc greater than the semicircle? Why?

A.why: Asks the student to work out the angle type; not a reflection.

B.why: Asks the student to work out the angle type for a major arc, so it is a task.

passages.text: Is the inscribed right angle inscribed in a semicircle? Explain your answer?

A.why: Asks the student to explain a converse; a task, not a reflection.

B.why: A question asking the student to work out and explain whether a right inscribed angle is in a semicircle, not a context or reflection.

lessons.title: Inscribed Angles Subtended by the Same Arc

objectives.label: Inscribed angles on the same arc
objectives.description: Find the measures of inscribed angles subtended by the same arc, and use their equality to solve for unknown angles and prove relations (e.g. equal segments).

objectives.label: Equal arcs, equal angles
objectives.description: Use equal arcs (and equal chords) in the same or congruent circles to show inscribed angles are equal, and the converse, to calculate unknowns and prove triangles isosceles.

objectives.label: Show points are concyclic
objectives.description: Decide whether four points lie on one circle by checking that two equal angles are drawn on the same base and on the same side of it.

passages.text: Are each two chords not intersecting inside a circle and subtended by two congruent arcs are parallel? Explain your answer.

A.why: It asks the student to decide and justify whether chords are parallel, so it is a task and not a reflection.

B.why: It asks the student to decide and explain whether the chords are parallel, which is work to do, not a reflection.

passages.text: What is the number of bisectors of $\angle BEC$? Explain your answer.

A.why: It asks the student to work out the number of bisectors, so it is a task.

B.why: It asks the student to work out and justify an answer, so it is not an introduction or a reflection.

passages.text: In the opposite figure, notice that: ∠C, ∠D are both drawn on the base AB, and on one side of it, m(∠C) = m(∠D). Then: The points A, B, C and D lie on one circle where AB is a chord in it.

A.why: The book states the idea that equal angles on the same base and the same side put four points on one circle, with no worked numbers.

B.why: It restates the rule for concyclic points as a note beside a figure, with no motivating situation.

passages.text: For More Exercises, go to MOE website

objectives.label: Identify cyclic quadrilaterals
objectives.description: Determine whether a given quadrilateral is a cyclic quadrilateral by checking whether two angles drawn on the same base and in one direction of it are equal, and explain the answer.

objectives.label: Prove a figure is cyclic
objectives.description: Prove that a figure is a cyclic quadrilateral by showing two equal angles (such as two right angles, or angles from parallel lines) on the same base and in one direction of it.

objectives.label: Use cyclic property in deductions
objectives.description: Use a proven cyclic quadrilateral and its circle to deduce equal angles, parallel lines and the location of the centre of the circle through its vertices.

passages.text: In the previous example, where is the center of the circle passing through the vertices of the figure AXBY? located? Explain your answer.

A.why: It asks the student to work out where the centre lies, so it is a question to solve and not an introduction or a look back.

B.why: It asks the student to work out where the centre is by explaining, so it is a question to solve, not a motivating context, introduction or reflection.

objectives.label: Opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral
objectives.description: Calculate unknown angles (and arcs) in a cyclic quadrilateral using the fact that each two opposite angles are supplementary.

objectives.label: Exterior angle of cyclic quadrilateral
objectives.description: Calculate angle measures using the corollary that the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior angle at the opposite vertex.

objectives.label: Prove a quadrilateral is cyclic
objectives.description: Prove that a quadrilateral is cyclic using the converse (supplementary opposite angles) or an exterior angle equal to the interior opposite angle.

passages.text: What do you notice on the sum of the two opposite angles in the cyclic quadrilateral?

A.why: Prompt asks what the student notices about opposite angles, setting up the supplementary fact before any numbers.

B.why: Asks what is noticed about opposite angles, introducing the idea that they are supplementary.

passages.text: Given: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. R.T.P: Prove that: (1) m(∠A) + m(∠C) = 180°; (2) m(∠B) + m(∠D) = 180°

A.why: This is the given and required-to-prove statement of a proof, not motivation.

B.why: The given and required-to-prove of a proof, a setup step.

passages.text: Proof: since m(∠A) = 1/2 m(arc BCD), and m(∠C) = 1/2 m(arc BAD), therefore m(∠A) + m(∠C) = 1/2 [m(arc BCD) + m(arc BAD)] = 1/2 × 360° = 180°. Similarly: m(∠B) + m(∠D) = 180° (Q.E.D.)

A.why: This is a worked proof step with numbers.

B.why: A step of the worked proof.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, E ∈ ray AB, E ∉ segment AB. ∴ ∠EBC is an angle outside the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠D is the inner angle opposite to it. Thus: m(∠EBC) = m(∠D) (The supplements of one angle is equal in measure)

A.why: This is a worked corollary derivation referring to a figure.

B.why: A corollary statement with its reasoning, a step of the book's derivation.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: if $m(\angle A)+m(\angle C)=180^\circ$ or $m(\angle B + m(\angle D) = 180^\circ$, so ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

A.why: This restates the converse as a formula or rule.

B.why: Restates the converse theorem as a formula/rule, not a motivating idea.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: ABCD is a quadrilateral, E ∈ ray AB, E ∉ segment AB. ∴ ∠EBC is an exterior angle at a vertex of the quadrilateral ABCD and ∠D is the inner angle opposite to it. If m(∠EBC) = m(∠D) then ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

A.why: This restates the exterior-angle converse as a rule.

B.why: States the converse exterior-angle rule as a formal statement, not a motivating intro.

passages.text: State the cases of the quadrilateral to be cyclic. Mention all the possible cases.

A.why: It asks the student to look back and list all the cases that make a quadrilateral cyclic.

B.why: Asks the student to look back and list all the cases that make a quadrilateral cyclic, after the converse work.

lessons.title: The relation between the tangents of a circle

objectives.label: Tangent segments from a point outside a circle
objectives.description: Use the equality of the two tangent segments drawn to a circle from a point outside it, and the corollaries (the line through the centre and the intersection point of the tangents is the axis of the chord of tangency and bisects the angle between the tangents), to find unknown lengths and angle measures and to prove relations.

objectives.label: Circle inscribed in a polygon
objectives.description: Use the circle inscribed in a polygon (touching all of its sides internally) and equal tangent segments to find the perimeter and area of the polygon and the position of the centre.

objectives.label: Common tangents of two circles
objectives.description: Distinguish common internal and common external tangents of two circles, and solve problems finding unknown values and the length of a common tangent.

passages.text: You know that the two tangents drawn at the two ends of a diameter in a circle are parallel.

A.why: Recalls the parallel tangents at a diameter's ends to lead into tangents at a chord's ends.

B.why: It recalls a known fact about tangents at the ends of a diameter to lead into tangents from a point.

passages.placed: the whole lesson: the readings named it and one objective

passages.text: In the opposite figure: Notice that: If AB is a chord in circle M, then the two tangents L1 and L2 intersect at the point C. Both CA and CB are called a tangent line segment and AB is called a chord of tangency.

A.why: Introduces what tangent segments and a chord of tangency are, with no worked numbers.

B.why: The book introduces tangent segments and the chord of tangency in words.

passages.text: Given: A is a point outside the circle M, AB and AC are two tangent segments of the circle at B and C. R.T.P: Prove that: AB = AC. onstruction: Draw MB, MC and MA.

A.why: Setup of the proof (given, to prove, construction).

B.why: It is the given and construction of a proof.

passages.text: Proof: ∵ AB is a tangent segment to circle M ∴ m(∠ABM) = 90°. ∵ AC is a tangent segment to circle M ∴ m(∠ACM) = 90°.

A.why: A step of the worked proof.

B.why: It is a step of a worked proof.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: Why is line MA the axis of BC?

A.why: Asks the student to explain a fact, which is work, not a reflection or an introduction.

B.why: It asks the student to work out a justification, so it does not look back on finished work.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: AB and AC are two tangents to circle M at B and C. Then: line AM is the axis of BC. Thus: AM ⊥ BC, and BD = CD

A.why: States a corollary result, a formula-like restatement.

B.why: It restates a corollary as a formula-like statement.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: AB and AC are two tangents to the circle M at B and C. Then: ray AM bisects ∠A, ∴ m(∠BAM) = m(∠CAM), ray MA bisects ∠BMC, ∴ m(∠AMB) = m(∠AMC)

A.why: States the angle-bisector corollary as a result.

B.why: It restates a corollary with symbols, with no motivating idea.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: AB and AC are two tangent segments to the circle M, $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}$, $m(\angle BMD) = 130^\circ$.

A.why: Figure setup for an example.

B.why: It is the setup of a figure for an exercise.

passages.text: M is the inscribed circle of the triangle ABC because it touches all of its sides internally at D, E and F. i.e.: The triangle ABC is drawn outside the circle M.

A.why: Introduces what an inscribed circle of a triangle is.

B.why: The book defines the inscribed circle of a triangle as one touching all sides internally.

passages.text: Is the center of the inscribed circle for any triangle the intersection point of the bisectors of its interior angles? Explain your answer.

A.why: Asks the student to work out and explain a claim, not a look back.

B.why: It asks the student to explain and justify a claim, so it is a question to work out, not a reflection on finished work.

passages.text: Why does ray AM bisect ∠BAC?
Why does ray MA bisect ∠BMC?

objectives.label: Calculate angles of tangency
objectives.description: Calculate the measure of an angle of tangency (or an unknown arc) using the fact that it is half the measure of the arc between its sides, and equals the inscribed angle on the same arc or half the central angle.

objectives.label: Prove cyclic quadrilaterals
objectives.description: Prove that a quadrilateral is cyclic by using the equality of the angle of tangency with the inscribed angle together with parallel lines.

objectives.label: Prove a line is tangent
objectives.description: Show that a line is a tangent to a circle by applying the converse of theorem 5 (angle with the chord equals the inscribed angle in the alternate side).

passages.text: In the opposite figure: $\angle ABC$ is an inscribed angle with the two sides $\overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ and arc $AC$, $\overrightarrow{BD}$ is a tangent to the circle at B. If we imagine the revolution of one of the sides of the inscribed angle, let it be $\overrightarrow{BC}$ moving away from $\overrightarrow{BA}$ so, it takes one of the positions $\overrightarrow{BC_1}$, $\overrightarrow{BC_2}$, ............

A.why: Introduces what an angle of tangency is by rotating a side of the inscribed angle toward the tangent, with no worked numbers.

B.why: Introduces the idea of an inscribed angle's side rotating until it becomes a tangent, with no worked numbers.

passages.text: Notice that: We get a larger inscribed angle in measure when $\overrightarrow{BC}$ and $\overrightarrow{BD}$ are about to be congruent. $\angle ABD$ is called the angle of tangency, it is a special case of the tangent angle:

A.why: Names the angle of tangency as the limiting case of the inscribed angle, saying what the idea is.

B.why: Names the angle of tangency as a special case of the tangent angle, introducing what it is.

passages.text: Given: ∠ABC is an angle of tangency and ∠D is an inscribed angle. R.T.P: Prove that $m(\angle ABC)=m(\angle D)$.

A.why: Given and required-to-prove statement of a theorem, part of the proof.

B.why: The given and required-to-prove of a theorem, a proof setup.

passages.text: Proof: ∵ ∠ABC is an angle of tangency ∴ $m(\angle ABC)=\frac{1}{2}m(\widehat{AB})$ (1). ∵ ∠D is an inscribed angle ∴ $m(\angle D)=\frac{1}{2}m(\widehat{AB})$ (2). From (1) and (2) we get: $m(\angle ABC)=m(\angle C)$. Q.E.D.

A.why: Steps of a worked proof.

B.why: The proof steps of the theorem.

passages.text: In the opposite figure: ray BC is tangent to circle M, AB is a chord of tangency. ∴ $m(\angle ABC)=m(\angle D)$ (theorem). ∵ $m(\angle D)=\frac{1}{2}m(\angle AMB)$ (theorem). ∴ $m(\angle ABC)=\frac{1}{2}m(\angle AMB)$.

A.why: A derivation restating a result from theorems, a worked step.

B.why: A step of a worked derivation relating the angle of tangency to the central angle.

passages.text: i.e.: If we draw ray AD from one end of the chord AB in circle M and m(∠DAB) = m(∠C) then: ray AD is a tangent to circle M.

A.why: Restates the converse theorem as a rule, a formula-type note.

B.why: A restatement of the converse theorem, not an intro or reflection.
